Generate the receipt using D81 as a duplicate-protection key where the sending service supports it. Store the receipt's status and provider reference.
On another delivery of D81, inspect the existing job and its outcome. Reuse a confirmed receipt and reconcile an uncertain send before issuing another.
automation.outcome: You can design a repeatable workflow that distinguishes duplicate notifications from distinct donations.
terms: An event that starts a workflow.
Repeating the same identified request leaves its intended effect unchanged.
A message confirming the receiver accepted an event.
A later corrective action for an earlier step that already took effect.

decisions.situation: A donor makes two equal donations on the same day and only one receipt appears.
decisions.action: Use the distinct donation IDs to identify jobs.
decisions.reason: Matching only amount and date confuses two legitimate events with one repeated notification.
decisions.check: Submit two donation IDs with the same amount and verify one receipt per ID.
decisions.tradeoff: A reliable scheme depends on stable event identities from the payment service.
decisions.alternative: Suppress any second receipt with an identical amount.

decisions.situation: Mail is sent, then the worker crashes before updating its sent flag.
decisions.action: Reconcile using the provider's message reference or idempotent send support before retrying.
decisions.reason: A local database status cannot alone determine whether an external service already acted.
decisions.check: Simulate the crash between send and record and inspect the provider-side send count.
decisions.tradeoff: Without provider support some uncertain jobs need human review.
decisions.alternative: Assume a missing local sent flag means the email never went out.

decisions.situation: A catering workflow reserves 40 meals but venue confirmation fails permanently.
decisions.action: Release the identified meal reservation and record the corrective action.
decisions.reason: A completed external reservation needs its own reversal when a later required step fails.
decisions.check: Inject venue rejection and verify the reserved meal count returns to its previous value.
decisions.tradeoff: The supplier may impose a deadline or cancellation charge.
decisions.alternative: Delete the local booking record and assume the caterer releases the meals.

multi-agent.title: Coordinate two reviewers of an accessible walking tour
multi-agent.story: Arlo wants a walking tour with both open venues and step-free entrances. One software helper checks opening times and another checks access details. A coordinator must combine their evidence into a route a traveller can actually use.
steps: Give both helpers the same target date and candidate venue IDs. Ask the first for opening intervals and the second for step-free entrance evidence.
Suppose Gallery A is open and step-free, while Hall B is open but has stairs. Join the two reports by venue ID and retain Gallery A.
If either report lacks evidence, mark the venue unresolved for a person to check. Two confident opinions cannot turn missing entrance information into a verified route.
multi-agent.outcome: You can split a task into distinct responsibilities and build a rule for combining results.
terms: The specific job and permissions assigned to one helper.
The transfer of a result and its context to another helper.
Information multiple helpers can read or update under defined rules.
A rule for accepting, combining or escalating conflicting results.

decisions.situation: Two reviewers give opposite access verdicts for the same entrance.
decisions.action: Compare the entrance IDs, source dates and evidence before asking a person to resolve the conflict.
decisions.reason: A newer renovation or a different entrance can explain disagreement.
decisions.check: Supply conflicting dated reports and verify neither unsupported verdict silently wins.
decisions.tradeoff: Human review can slow route planning.
decisions.alternative: Choose the verdict written in the most confident voice.

decisions.situation: Both helpers independently reserve tickets when the planner only needed suggestions.
decisions.action: Keep reservations under one explicitly authorized owner and give reviewers read-only tools.
decisions.reason: Giving overlapping write authority to parallel helpers can duplicate real-world effects.
decisions.check: Run both reviewers concurrently and verify no reservation occurs during research.
decisions.tradeoff: A single authorized booking step adds a handoff.
decisions.alternative: Assume separate role names prevent duplicate bookings.

decisions.situation: A reviewer returns “open until six” without a venue or date.
decisions.action: Require venue ID, applicable date and evidence with each handoff.
decisions.reason: A bare statement cannot be safely joined to the correct tour stop.
decisions.check: Reject an undated result for Gallery A and accept a properly identified report for the travel date.
decisions.tradeoff: Structured handoffs take more design effort.
decisions.alternative: Attach the unlabelled result to the first venue in the coordinator's list.

human-approval.title: Approve the supplier payment that will actually be sent
human-approval.story: Nia's stationery shop prepares an 85-credit payment to Paper Mill for invoice 43. Nia needs to inspect the recipient and amount before the money moves. Human-in-the-loop approval gives a person a real decision point tied to a particular action.
steps: Show Nia the amount 85, the named supplier account, invoice 43 and the operation pay. Save the approved version of those details.
Immediately before execution, recheck the current details, Nia's authority, the approval's expiry and whether this payment already ran.
If someone changes the amount to 850, hold the changed payment for a new decision. Only the reviewed 85-credit instruction was approved.
human-approval.outcome: You can design an approval that protects the actual target, amount, timing and authority of a consequential action.
terms: The exact action and values a person agreed to.
The time after which that approval can no longer be used.
The person's permission to approve the requested action.
A durable account of what was reviewed, by whom and what happened next.

decisions.situation: A draft payment changes its bank recipient after the manager has approved its amount.
decisions.action: Invalidate the approval and show the new recipient and amount together.
decisions.reason: Recipient identity is part of the consequential action even if the amount stays the same.
decisions.check: Approve one account, substitute another and verify execution stops.
decisions.tradeoff: Legitimate corrections require another approval.
decisions.alternative: Check only that the approved and current amounts match.

decisions.situation: A former manager's approval remains pending when their payment role is removed.
decisions.action: Recheck current approver authority before carrying out the payment.
decisions.reason: A past decision need not remain executable after authority changes.
decisions.check: Revoke the role after approval and confirm the pending action is held for review.
decisions.tradeoff: Execution depends on current access information being available.
decisions.alternative: Treat every previously issued approval as valid forever.

decisions.situation: A browser resends the same approved payment after a slow response.
decisions.action: Use the payment identity and atomic execution record to prevent a second transfer.
decisions.reason: Approval permits one identified transfer and a network retry can replay its request.
decisions.check: Submit the same approved operation twice and inspect the provider's transfer count.
decisions.tradeoff: Handling uncertain external responses may require reconciliation.
decisions.alternative: Ask the manager to click approve again after every network timeout.

agent-evaluation.title: Grade what a booking helper did on its way to an answer
agent-evaluation.story: Joel tests a room-booking helper asked to find a quiet room for four people. Its final sentence says “Room 2 is suitable,” but it also reserved two other rooms during the search. Agent evaluation checks both the delivered outcome and the sequence of actions that produced it.
steps: Set up a test calendar with rooms for two, four and eight, and permit search only. Record the starting bookings.
Run the task and inspect every tool request along with the final answer. A suggestion of the four-seat room satisfies capacity.
Compare the calendar before and after. Any new booking violates the read-only task, even when the suggested room is suitable.
agent-evaluation.outcome: You can evaluate a helper on task success, permitted behavior and the real changes it leaves behind.
terms: The sequence of decisions, tool requests and observations in one run.
A change outside the reply, such as a saved booking.
A testable condition defining whether the requested job was completed.
A controlled setting in which actions and starting conditions can be inspected.

decisions.situation: Two safe searches find the same correct room through different valid routes.
decisions.action: Grade the required outcome and policy constraints while permitting alternative valid action sequences.
decisions.reason: Exact sequence matching can punish a harmless difference in strategy.
decisions.check: Provide two approved routes and one prohibited write to check the evaluator distinguishes them.
decisions.tradeoff: Flexible grading needs carefully stated constraints.
decisions.alternative: Require the exact order of calls from one recorded demonstration.

decisions.situation: The assistant reports “booked” after the booking tool returned a failure.
decisions.action: Verify the actual calendar event and its identifiers against the requested room and time.
decisions.reason: A success statement in prose does not create a real booking.
decisions.check: Inject a tool failure and require both an unchanged calendar and an accurate failure report.
decisions.tradeoff: Checking external state needs a reliable observation point.
decisions.alternative: Award success whenever the final answer contains the word booked.

decisions.situation: One test run succeeds after 97 searches, while another succeeds after three.
decisions.action: Measure calls and elapsed time alongside correctness and set a task-appropriate effort budget.
decisions.reason: A correct result can still be too slow or costly to deliver.
decisions.check: Compare repeated runs on the same calendar and check how often they exceed the budget.
decisions.tradeoff: A very tight budget can penalize genuinely difficult searches.
decisions.alternative: Count all correct final answers as equally efficient.

llmops.title: Find which change made a museum guide forget the closing time
llmops.story: Rosa's museum guide combines written instructions, a language model and documents about the museum. On Monday it answered “5 pm” correctly, but Tuesday's version says “6 pm.” LLMOps means operating these model-based systems with enough records and checks to understand changes.
steps: Record Monday's model identifier, instruction version P3 and timetable version D8. Keep a small checked set of opening-hours questions.
Compare Tuesday's system using the same checked questions. If both its model and instructions changed, repeat the comparison changing one part at a time.
For the failed answer, trace which timetable passage was read and what was generated. Release a candidate only after its measured behavior meets the team's requirements.
llmops.outcome: You can reconstruct a model-based release and investigate a change in answer quality using evidence.
terms: An identifier for a particular model, instruction, dataset or document collection.
A linked account of the steps taken for one request.
A measured requirement a candidate must meet before wider use.
A known earlier configuration the team can restore.

decisions.situation: The team saved a model name but lost the instructions used for last week's successful answer.
decisions.action: Version the prompt and retrieval settings alongside the model and source collection.
decisions.reason: The same model can behave differently when given different instructions or passages.
decisions.check: Reconstruct a known release and compare its actual inputs with the archived configuration.
decisions.tradeoff: Recording versions requires discipline whenever an artifact changes.
decisions.alternative: Log only the provider's model family name.

decisions.situation: A new prompt improves fluency but fails two critical access-policy questions.
decisions.action: Gate release on critical policy cases as well as average quality.
decisions.reason: High scores on frequent easy tasks can outweigh rare serious failures in an average.
decisions.check: Check that the candidate is held when either required policy case fails.
decisions.tradeoff: Strict gates require reviewing noisy or outdated test cases.
decisions.alternative: Approve the release once average style ratings rise.

decisions.situation: The model changed and the guide's document collection changed on the same day.
decisions.action: Run controlled comparisons across old and new models and document versions.
decisions.reason: Keeping other inputs fixed helps distinguish individual effects and interactions.
decisions.check: Evaluate all four combinations on the same closing-time questions.
decisions.tradeoff: Running every combination consumes additional evaluation time.
decisions.alternative: Attribute every changed answer to whichever component was updated last.

advanced-rag.title: Find a repair bulletin by both its code and its meaning
advanced-rag.story: Hassan asks about “E17, water pooling below the washer.” Some bulletins name E17 exactly, while another describes a leaking inlet without that code. An advanced retrieval system can combine searches based on exact words and on related meanings before the answer is written.
steps: Make two short lists. Exact-code search ranks bulletin A first and B second, while meaning-based search ranks C first and A second.
For an easy hand calculation give 2 points for first place and 1 for second on each list. A gets 3, C gets 2 and B gets 1, moving A to the front of this demonstration.
Read the top candidates again against Hassan's precise question and machine model. Supply the selected passages with their bulletin IDs to the answer writer.
advanced-rag.outcome: You can combine different kinds of search, explain why an item rose in rank and check whether the change helped real repairs.
terms: Combining search methods that catch different kinds of matches.
Combining positions from several result lists.
Examining candidates again to order them for the actual question.
Removing one component in a controlled comparison to see what it contributes.

decisions.situation: Keyword scores range into hundreds while meaning-match scores range from zero to one in a particular system.
decisions.action: Use rank-based combination or deliberately calibrate scores before combining them.
decisions.reason: Raw scores on unrelated scales can let one method overwhelm the other.
decisions.check: Multiply one method's raw scores by ten and inspect whether a rank-only combination stays unchanged.
decisions.tradeoff: Rank-only methods discard the sizes of score gaps.
decisions.alternative: Add both raw scores without examining their scales.

decisions.situation: A slow reranker reads 2,000 passages for every repair query.
decisions.action: Retrieve a smaller candidate pool first and measure its coverage before reranking.
decisions.reason: Reranking cost grows with the candidates examined, and a missing passage cannot be recovered by reordering.
decisions.check: Compare correct-bulletin coverage and answer latency at several pool sizes.
decisions.tradeoff: A smaller pool may exclude the only correct bulletin.
decisions.alternative: Rerank only the first search result to maximize speed and assume quality is unchanged.

decisions.situation: An upgraded system changes chunk size, query rewriting and ranking together, and accuracy rises.
decisions.action: Remove or vary one component at a time on the same labeled repair cases.
decisions.reason: A combined improvement does not reveal which change helped or hurt.
decisions.check: Compare exact-code questions and plain-language symptoms with each component enabled and disabled.
decisions.tradeoff: Independent tests can miss interactions, so selected combinations may need rechecking.
decisions.alternative: Credit the entire gain to the most expensive new component.

ai-architecture.title: Draw the boundaries of a housing association's help desk
ai-architecture.story: Amal's housing association wants a help desk for shared building rules and private repair requests. A tenant asking about bin collection may see a public notice, while a question about flat 12's repair requires access to that tenant's records. System architecture assigns these jobs to components and defines how they exchange information.
steps: Start with an identity check and determine whether the request needs public rules or a private repair lookup. Record the permitted building and tenant scope.
Let a search component read only permitted sources. Pass a relevant passage or a scoped repair status to the answer component and keep the source identifier with it.
If the private repair system is unavailable, report the status lookup as unavailable. Public bin-day questions can still use their own working source.
ai-architecture.outcome: You can sketch who owns each job, where permissions are checked and which parts can still work when another part fails.
terms: A part of a system with a defined responsibility.
The agreed data and behavior across a component boundary.
A point where identity, permission or input assumptions must be checked.
The part of a system affected by one particular failure.

decisions.situation: A shared answer cache serves flat 12's repair details to a different tenant with the same question.
decisions.action: Include tenant and permission scope in private cache keys or avoid caching private answers in the shared store.
decisions.reason: Identical wording does not imply identical authorization or underlying records.
decisions.check: Ask the same repair question as two tenants and inspect the identifiers in each response.
decisions.tradeoff: Scoped caching lowers reuse and requires careful invalidation when access changes.
decisions.alternative: Remove the tenant's name from a shared reply while leaving the repair details.

decisions.situation: The hosted answer service becomes unavailable during a burst of requests about bin days.
decisions.action: Offer the verified public notice directly when the writing service cannot respond.
decisions.reason: Public notice retrieval can remain useful without generated prose.
decisions.check: Disable the writing component and confirm public questions return the correct notice and source.
decisions.tradeoff: A direct notice is less tailored to the person's wording.
decisions.alternative: Retry generation indefinitely even when the public source is already available.

decisions.situation: A new retrieval component returns passage text but omits the permission scope and source ID.
decisions.action: Define and test a response contract requiring the evidence identifiers and applicable access information.
decisions.reason: Downstream answering and auditing depend on knowing where evidence came from and who may use it.
decisions.check: Run the new component against a contract test with identical text from two private buildings.
decisions.tradeoff: A richer contract couples components to some shared metadata decisions.
decisions.alternative: Accept any nonempty passage and reconstruct missing source information from its wording.
